title: Solvei
summary: A skincare line with nine products and no interest in shouting. The identity had to survive a 12mm label and still read across a shelf.
imageAlt: Three matte ceramic skincare bottles on a pale plaster ledge
outcome: Nine SKUs shipped in one production run. Retail listings in four countries within a quarter.
quote: It is the first time our packaging has looked like the thing inside it.
content:
Solvei came to me with a formulation they were proud of and a bottle they were not. The brief was framed as a packaging job. Two conversations in it was clear the actual problem was that nobody at the company could say, in one sentence, what made the products different — which is why every label draft ended up carrying four sentences.

Finding the sentence

We spent the first week interviewing the chemist rather than the founders. What came out of it was unglamorous and useful: the formulations are deliberately short. Six ingredients where a competitor uses twenty. That was the whole identity, sitting in a spreadsheet nobody had thought to show a designer.

So the system got short too. One weight of one typeface. A number on the front, the ingredient count, set larger than the product name. No adjectives anywhere on the primary panel — they moved to the back, where someone standing in a shop has actually decided to read.

Designing for 12 millimetres

The serum is the smallest bottle in the range and it drove every decision. If the mark did not survive at 12mm it did not exist. We tested every candidate as a laser-etched sample before drawing anything at full size, which killed three directions in a morning and saved about a month.

The constraint that looks like a limitation is usually the brief. The serum label was the brief.

What shipped

Nine products, one production run, a set of rules short enough that the founder can lay out a new SKU herself in an afternoon. That last part was the real deliverable. A system nobody can operate is a rebrand with an expiry date.

title: Fold
summary: A savings app for people who find money stressful. We redesigned around the two screens that actually get opened, and deleted most of the rest.
imageAlt: A smartphone on a pale oak desk showing a minimal finance dashboard
outcome: Weekly active use up 41%. Support tickets about the dashboard down to almost none.
quote: She cut half the product and it got bigger. I still think about that.
content:
Fold had eleven tabs. The analytics said people used two of them. Everyone at the company knew this and nobody wanted to be the one who suggested deleting the other nine, because each one had been somebody's quarter.

Reading the sessions

We watched forty session recordings before opening a design file. The pattern was not subtle: people opened the app, looked at one number, felt something about it, and left. Median session length was under nine seconds. Everything we had been designing assumed a user who was browsing. There was no browsing.

That reframed the job. The dashboard was not a hub, it was a glance. So it got one number, set enormous, with the context underneath in a size you only read if you have decided to care. Everything else moved behind a single second screen.

Designing the bad days

Financial products are mostly designed for the good state — the balance going up and to the right. The screens people actually remember are the other ones. We drew the overdraft, the failed transfer, the month where the number goes the wrong way, and we drew them first.

Tone did most of the work. No red. No exclamation marks. A failed transfer says what happened and what happens next, in that order, and nothing else. It sounds small; it changed the support queue more than any feature we shipped.

The handover

The system went over as forty-one components with every state drawn, including the ones nobody asks for. The engineering lead's note afterwards was that they had not needed to invent a single screen. That is the metric I care about.

title: Marrow Roasters
summary: A roastery that wanted to stop looking like a roastery. One mark, one paper stock, and a numbering system that does the branding for us.
imageAlt: A kraft coffee bag with a die-cut geometric mark beside scattered beans
outcome: One bag, one sticker, thirty-plus rotating lots. Print costs down by roughly a third.
quote: We print one bag now instead of nine. Nobody warned me that was the design.
content:
Specialty coffee has a house style and Marrow was tired of it. Not the taste — the look. Every bag on the shelf was doing the same thing: an illustration of a mountain, a paragraph about a farm, four tasting notes in a row.

The economics were the brief

Marrow rotates thirty-odd lots a year. Under the old system each one needed its own printed bag, which meant minimum orders, which meant a cupboard full of packaging for coffee that had already sold out. The design problem was actually an inventory problem.

So the bag stopped carrying the coffee's identity. One kraft bag, one die-cut mark, printed once in volume. The lot lives on a single applied label: a number, an origin, a date. The system's variety comes from the labels, which cost almost nothing and can be printed the morning a lot lands.

A mark that survives a die

The mark had to work as a physical hole in a bag, which rules out most of what a mark can be. No fine lines, no counters under 3mm, no dependence on colour. What survived is a shape you can cut, emboss, stencil onto a window or stamp on a cup — which turned out to be the whole signage system too.

We designed the cheapest version first. Everything good about the system came out of that constraint rather than in spite of it.

In the shop

The same shape scaled up to the shop front, cut once out of steel. It is the only piece of the identity that cost real money, and it is the only piece that needed to.

title: Atrium Studio
summary: An architecture practice whose old site made their buildings look small. We gave the photographs the whole screen and got out of the way.
imageAlt: An open laptop on a travertine table showing a spacious minimal website
outcome: Enquiries doubled in the first quarter. Two of them named a specific project on the site.
quote: Our work finally looks the size it is.
content:
Atrium's photography is extraordinary and their old website showed it at 380 pixels wide inside a card with a drop shadow. That was the entire diagnosis. It took ten minutes and the rest of the project was carrying it out properly.

One decision, held

Every image runs to the edge of the viewport. No cards, no frames, no shadows, no rounded corners on anything that contains a photograph. The interface is a thin layer of type that appears when you need it and recedes when you do not.

Holding that meant saying no to a lot of reasonable requests. A filter bar. A related-projects grid. A newsletter block over the imagery. Each one was defensible on its own and each one would have re-introduced the frame we had just removed.

Making it fast anyway

Full-bleed photography is the easiest way to build a slow website. Every image ships in three sizes as AVIF with a JPEG fallback, decoded off the main thread, with the first viewport's image preloaded and everything below it deferred. The project pages weigh less than the old card grid did.

Writing the captions

The other half of the job was text. Architecture sites tend toward the abstract — a dialogue between volume and light. We replaced all of it with facts: where it is, what it was before, how many people use it, what it is made of. It reads better and it ranks better, which was not the point but was not unwelcome either.

title: Vellum Press
summary: A cover system for an independent press publishing twelve books a year on a budget that allowed one photograph, total.
imageAlt: Four slim hardback books with plain uncoated covers, one spine in lime
outcome: Twenty-two titles on the system so far. Each cover takes about a day.
quote: The rules make the decisions now, so we argue about the books instead.
content:
Vellum publishes essays and short criticism — the kind of books that live or die on whether someone picks them up in a shop. They had no photography budget and no illustration budget, and twelve titles a year to design.

Typography as the whole image

With no imagery, the type has to carry the emotional weight, which most cover typography is not asked to do. We built a system with exactly three variables: the size of the title relative to the trim, its vertical position, and one colour from a fixed set of six uncoated inks.

Three variables is enough for hundreds of distinct covers and few enough that a junior designer produces something correct on their first attempt. That was deliberate. The system had to survive me leaving.

The spine test

Every cover is designed spine-first. In a real shop, face-out is a privilege that maybe two titles a season get. If the spine does not work, the book does not exist — so the spine is drawn before the front, and any front that compromises it is wrong by definition.

Design the worst-case display condition first and the good ones take care of themselves.

Ink and paper

Six inks on one uncoated stock, chosen so that any two sit next to each other on a shelf without fighting. The lime is the loudest and it is rationed to one title a season. Restraint that is written into the system is the only kind that survives contact with a launch.

title: Northbound
summary: Cycling apparel for people who ride to work rather than race. The identity had to work stitched, printed, reflective, and 4mm tall.
imageAlt: A folded technical cycling jersey beside an aluminium bottle, overhead view
outcome: Two collections shipped on the system. Reflective mark visible at roughly 80 metres.
quote: We stopped designing each garment from scratch. That is months a year back.
content:
Most cycling brands design for the podium and sell to commuters. Northbound wanted to skip the pretence: the clothes are for a wet Tuesday and an eleven-kilometre ride to an office where you have to look normal afterwards.

Four production methods, one mark

The mark had to be embroidered, screen printed, heat transferred, and cut in reflective vinyl. Each method has a different minimum feature size, and the smallest of them governs. We drew to the embroidery limit and everything else came for free.

That is why it is a shape rather than a wordmark. A wordmark at 4mm stitched is a smudge, and a smudge on a garment is worse than no mark at all.

Reflectivity as design, not safety theatre

The visible identity in daylight is quiet — a tonal shape on the chest. At night, under a headlight, the same shape lights up along with a band across the shoulders. It is the same graphic doing two jobs, which meant one placement to develop rather than a separate safety treatment bolted on.

The system in the factory

The deliverable that mattered was a placement grid: for any garment, where the mark goes, at what size, in which method, with the tolerances the factory actually works to. It is four pages. It has removed roughly a month of back-and-forth per collection.
